title: The compassionate heart
hookLine: Jayadeva sings the Buddha in Vishnu's line, and two traditions stop at the frightened animal
carry: ahimsa: don't harm what fears harm
tomorrow: the Bhagavata gives the Buddha a single verse. what does it say?

lines: WHAT DOES A KIND HEART SEE?
cards: Some people will stop a whole conversation to carry a spider outside in a cup instead of squashing it. Ask why and the answer is usually short: it didn't do anything to me.
Now count Vishnu's forms the way some Hindu lists do. Fish, tortoise, boar, man-lion, dwarf, Rama with the axe, Rama with the bow, Krishna. Then a name that surprises people: the Buddha.
One Hindu poet sings him with a single quality, the same one behind the spider in the cup. So today's question: what does a compassionate heart see?

teach.b: The poet is Jayadeva, and the hymn is in his Gita Govinda, one verse for each of Vishnu's forms.

His Buddha verse says, in plain English: with a compassionate heart, having seen the killing of animals, you find fault with the rules of sacrifice. The Sanskrit is sadaya hridaya, a heart with compassion in it.
That's Jayadeva's answer: compassion sees the creature at the altar.
Now hear the Buddha's own followers, in their own book, the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death."
The verse goes on: see yourself in them, and don't kill or cause killing. So here is one thing shared, each in its own words: whatever fears harm is like you, so don't harm it.
In Sanskrit that's ahimsa, not harming. And here's the honest difference, which matters just as much.
Buddhists don't count the Buddha as a descent of Vishnu.
He's their own teacher, the Awakened One, and his life is theirs to tell. Jayadeva's verse even has the Buddha faulting the Vedic sacrifice, while Hindus keep the Vedas as scripture.
Two traditions, two maps of who he is, and both of them stopping at the same frightened animal.

how: Jayadeva's hymn of the ten forms is sung in some Hindu temples and homes, the Buddha verse among them; Buddhists honor the Buddha as their own teacher and recite the Dhammapada's verses in their own practice.

o: the Awakened One, told by Hindus and Buddhists their own ways
a sage who wrote down the hymn of Vishnu's ten forms
a king of the Kali age who put an end to sacrifice

games.q: two traditions, their own words — tap the pairs.
p: a heart with compassion in it

s: Buddhists count the Buddha as a descent of Vishnu
that's a Hindu telling; Buddhists tell him as their own teacher.
Jayadeva sings the Buddha as moved by animals killed at the altar
sadaya hridaya: a heart with compassion in it.
if two traditions share an idea, they're really the same religion
they can share care for living things and still tell very different stories about the Buddha.

games.q: Dawa invites you to a festival meal at her family's temple. an aunt asks what Hindus think of the Buddha. what's a fair answer?
o: some Hindu texts honor him in Vishnu's line; I know you tell his story your own way.
Hindus see him as Vishnu, so really he's part of our religion, not yours.
Hindus don't really have anything to say about the Buddha at all.
games.why: say who tells what: some Hindu texts honor him as Vishnu's descent; Buddhists tell him as their teacher. neither telling has to swallow the other.

practice: Rest your eyes on one living thing you can see: a plant, a pet, a bird outside, or your own hand with its pulse. Watch it for the sit, breathing slowly, and notice that it, too, would pull back from harm.
Let your gaze be gentle with it.

wordCard.voice: Buddha: in some Hindu lists, a descent of Vishnu; in Jayadeva's verse, the one with the compassionate heart. Buddhists tell him as their own teacher, the Awakened One.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: Buddha, the title Buddhists give their teacher, the Awakened One.

carryVoice: Keep this: ahimsa, don't harm what fears harm. Jayadeva's Buddha stopped at the creature on the altar. See you tomorrow.
